messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Javier, a 62-year-old psychiatrist, carried his past with a quiet, practiced composure that was beginning to fray at the edges. Thirty years ago, in his home country, his work at a public health clinic that served political dissidents had drawn the attention of the ruling regime. He was taken from his home one night by men in uniform. The weeks that followed were a blur of sensory torment: the rough, suffocating hood that smelled of mould; the cold concrete floor; and most of all, the sounds—a cacophony of overlapping, urgent questions from multiple interrogators, their words tangling into an incomprehensible threat that was more terrifying than any single statement. He never saw their faces clearly, but their voices, layered and menacing, became etched into his mind. He was eventually released after international pressure, and he rebuilt his life and career in the United States, but the interrogation room had never fully let him go.

For decades, Javier managed to keep the memories contained. But in the last year, something had shifted. Watching a news report on political prisoners in another part of the world was the first crack. The televised image of a man in a uniform was all it took to instantly bring back the full memory, not as a recollection but as a re-experiencing. Suddenly, he was no longer in his living room but back on the damp floor, the phantom scent of stale water in his nostrils and the garbled, accusatory chatter filling his ears. These intrusions were terrifyingly vivid and unpredictable; something as innocuous as passing a security guard in the lobby of his own hospital could trigger a fragment, plunging him back into that state of helpless terror.

The content of these memories relentlessly fed a set of deeply held, painful beliefs. Each time he relived his powerlessness, it was a visceral confirmation that the institutions that should have protected him—his government, international bodies, even his own profession—had utterly failed. This conviction that the people responsible had faced no consequences, and that the world was fundamentally unjust, seemed to keep the memories close to the surface, as if his mind were constantly scanning for proof of this betrayal and finding it in the past. His pervasive sense of institutional failure made him exquisitely sensitive to any sign of authority, and because he was certain that people in uniform were a source of danger, he found himself constantly scanning for them, making encounters with police or security guards feel both inevitable and perilous.

The sheer sensory force of the memories drove him to shrink his world. After one particularly harrowing flashback, triggered by the overlapping conversations in a crowded cafe, he began to avoid going out unless absolutely necessary. The memory of the interrogators' voices was so distressing that afterward, even the sound of two people talking at once in the hospital cafeteria felt threatening, expanding his list of what to avoid. To manage the anxiety of necessary interactions, he started to meticulously rehearse what he would say before any meeting with a colleague or even a simple phone call with a patient's family. He believed this preparation was a shield against being caught off guard, but it left him feeling stilted and disconnected, a mere actor playing the part of a psychiatrist.

This retreat into avoidance and rehearsal only tightened the trap. By turning down invitations from friends and staying away from cultural events he once cherished, his isolation became concrete proof of his most painful appraisal: that he had lost his connection to his community and culture. His constant rehearsal of conversations, a strategy meant to control his anxiety, instead made him hyper-aware of auditory stimuli; as a result, the sound of incomprehensible chatter from a nearby television became an almost physical assault. His attempts to cope by quickly thinking of something else when a memory started to surface were also backfiring; the suppressed fragments would only return later with more intensity, as if demanding to be felt.

Javier came to therapy after a consultation with a young resident. As the resident spoke, another doctor interrupted with a question, and for a moment their voices overlapped. Javier froze, his mind blank. He felt the familiar dread rise, the phantom pressure of the hood. He could not follow the conversation and had to abruptly end the meeting, claiming he felt unwell. The incident crystallized his fear: the very tools of his trade—listening, speaking, being present for others—were being dismantled by his past. He felt he was not only failing his patients but losing the core of his own identity. He came to his first session not with hope, but with a quiet desperation to stop his world from shrinking into nothing more than the four walls of that long-ago room.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not describe a causal link where a trigger directly influences or leads to a negative appraisal.
